notes.body:
The ruling turns on a precise question: can an obligation be discharged when its proper recipient does not exist? The text presents two edge cases side by side — the man whose debt cancels his asset, and the polytheist who owes purifying alms (زكاة) but has no Muslim to give them to. When the condition for fulfilling an obligation is absent, **the obligation cannot move forward**.

The jurisprudential principle at work is the concept of a legitimate channel (مصرف) — a qualified recipient through whom the duty flows. The Quran itself names eight categories of people who may receive alms (زكاة); if none of those categories is present, there is no lawful direction in which the wealth can travel. The payer is not released from duty; **the duty is frozen in place**.

This is why the text says the polytheist "has more right to it than anyone else." It is not a cancellation of the debt he owes to Allah — **no valid transfer can occur** when the receiving end of the transaction is missing. Think of a bill that is due but the creditor's office is closed: you still owe the money, but you cannot legally hand it over until the office reopens.

In Ismaili thought, this ruling deepens when the role of the Imam is brought in. The Mustansiriyya sessions teach that alms (زكاة) must be delivered to the Imam (ع) or to whoever he has appointed. **The chain of delivery is not a formality** — it is part of the obligation itself. A polytheist who enters Islam in a place without any Imam-connected community has no operative end of that chain, and his obligation is suspended, not dissolved.

**The moment a qualified recipient or the Imam's representative becomes accessible, the duty revives in full.** The wealth that remained with the payer was never truly his to keep; it was held in custody until the legitimate channel (مصرف) opened.

notes.quote: a man among the polytheists who has found no Muslim to whom to hand the zakat of his wealth, so he has more right to it than anyone else
etymology: زكاة (purifying alms): from root ز-ك-و, meaning to grow and to be pure. The same root gives both increase and cleanliness — because paying alms purifies what remains and causes it to spiritually multiply. The word holds both meanings at once, which is why giving feels, paradoxically, like gaining.

مصرف (legitimate channel): from root ص-ر-ف, to turn or divert a flow. A مصرف is where wealth is deliberately 'turned toward' — the valid recipient who receives and redirects it. The root conveys purposeful re-routing, not random dispersal.

أهلية (eligibility): from root أ-ه-ل, the word for family or household — those who inherently belong. Legal eligibility means belonging to a recognized category. A recipient must 'belong' to a qualifying group before any transfer of wealth is lawful.

واجب (obligation): from root و-ج-ب, to fall due — like something that tips and can no longer be held upright. An obligation has 'fallen upon' a person and must be discharged. The imagery of falling gives the term its sense of urgency and weight.
